messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Daniel, a 36‑year‑old tax consultant who has been married for eight years, sits at his desk in the quiet corner of a downtown office, staring at a spreadsheet while his wife’s voice buzzes in his ear about the wedding plans. He can feel his heart racing in his chest and his stomach turning over the same memory that has haunted him since his last deployment. The weight of that memory presses down on him like a physical load, making even the routine of filing paperwork feel like a battleground. The incident that set the trajectory of Daniel’s current distress happened in the summer of 2015, on a dusty field in Iraq. He was in a squad that had just taken cover from a mortar strike when an improvised explosive device detonated behind them. The blast sent shrapnel into the air, and a close friend collapsed, clutching a torn piece of uniform. Daniel heard the scream that followed and, for a split second, saw the taste of metal and blood on his tongue—an image that has since become part of every flashback. The sound of a single word—“clear”—suddenly echoed as a warning, and the sudden silence that followed felt like a shroud of danger. Because of that experience, Daniel now associates conflict in the office with the sound of a client’s raised voice. When a client confronts him about a deduction he feels is wrong, the echo of his friend’s scream pushes him into a state of alarm. That alarm triggers his tendency to avoid being touched; the sudden brush of a colleague’s hand on his arm reminds him of the startle to touch he feels whenever someone unexpectedly touches him. The avoidance of touch feeds back into his sense that the workplace is hostile, so he steers clear of situations where physical contact might happen, such as joint meetings or informal gatherings. The topics of conversation that trigger Daniel are not limited to conflict. When a client mentions a change in tax law, Daniel’s mind flares with images of the battlefield, and the taste of metal and blood floods back, overwhelming him. The recall is so vivid that he must stop and breathe, trying to steady his shaking hands. This overwhelm leads him to avoid talking about the event at all; his silence, in the sense that he chooses to stay quiet, feels like a threat, a danger that could arise at any moment. The silence he experiences when his wife asks about his war, or when a coworker shares a joke, forces him to plan escape routes in his mind—mental ways out of the room or out of the conversation—before he can feel comfortable. Each time a conversation topic or a moment of conflict brings the memory back, Daniel’s fear escalates. He finds himself feeling ill, nauseous and physically unwell, a bodily reaction that reminds him of the chaos of that day. The physical illness, in turn, reinforces his belief that the situation is dangerous, tightening the loop of threat. The threat of silence, the fear of being touched, and the anticipation of confrontation all act like an alarm that never stops. Daniel has learned that every time he feels that startle to touch, his memory flashes again, and the images of blood and metal swirl so strongly that he must leave the room to regain composure. His avoidance of positive feelings—such as a brief compliment from a client—also fuels his sense of threat; accepting praise feels unsafe, as if the world could turn hostile in an instant. This cycle has taken a toll on Daniel’s professional and personal life. He now arrives late to important meetings because he spends extra time mapping out escape routes. The constant planning has left him exhausted, and the physical illness that follows a confrontation has begun to strain his relationship with his wife, who worries that his silence means he is withdrawing from their future. He has stopped celebrating his wife’s birthday because the joy feels too close to the hurt he carries; any positive emotion is a threat that he must push away. The decision to seek help came after a client asked him in a firm tone if he was still “on the job.” Daniel felt his stomach drop; the sense that his life was again a battleground made him freeze. He realized he could no longer ignore the relentless loop of triggers, threats, memory, and avoidance that controlled his days. Daniel now fears that if he does not address the loop, he will lose the life he has worked so hard to build, but he also hopes that a therapist can help him untangle the chain that has bound him to the battlefield’s echo.
